clips.title: Claude Code's New Eval Tool: Do Skills Actually Work?
clips.why: Someone ran five real skills through claude plugin eval against plain Claude, the same comparison this lesson teaches, and shows the scoreboard first.
look: The scoreboard: notice how many skills scored about the same as plain Claude. A skill that reads well is not automatically a skill that helps.
How the command works: the same prompts and graders, run with the skill and without it.
What made the one skill that clearly helped different from the others.
clips.after: Our plugin CI runs this same with-and-without comparison on every plugin change, so a skill that ties or loses to plain Claude is visible before it reaches every laptop and Nova.

clips.title: Claude Code's New Eval Tool: Do Skills Actually Work?
clips.why: The skill that scored lower than no skill, and a grader that gave the wrong verdict: the two surprises an eval is for.
look: A negative difference means the skill made results worse on that task.
Before blaming the skill, check the grader: a judge can mark a good answer wrong.
clips.after: That is why our gate fails a plugin whose mean difference is below zero, and why a judge is checked against people's own labels before it decides anything.

clips.title: LLM as a Judge: Scaling AI Evaluation Strategies
clips.why: A plain explanation of when a model can grade another model's answers, and the biases that make it wrong.
look: A judge scales: it reads thousands of answers a person never could.
The drawbacks and biases he lists. Two common ones are a preference for longer answers and for the option shown first.
Think about what would make a judge trustworthy despite those biases.
clips.after: In our suites free graders run on every pull request and judges run nightly, each judge written as concrete PASS and FAIL conditions.

practice.q: A case scores 1.00 with the plugin and 1.00 without it. What does that tell you?

options.text: The skill works perfectly on this task
options.why: Claude did just as well without the skill, so the score says nothing about the skill.

options.text: The skill adds nothing on this task: Claude already does it well alone
options.why: Δ is 0. Either the case is too easy to show the skill's value, or this part of the skill is not needed and could be cut.

options.text: The graders are broken and must be rewritten
options.why: Perfect scores in both arms are a common, real result. Look at the prompt first: does it test what the skill adds?

practice.q: Finish the grader so a goodbye request must not load welcome-note, and the check counts in both arms.
practice.before:
type: tool_used
tool: Skill
input_match: '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?welcome-note"'
min: 0
max: 0
arm:
practice.hint: One word: the opposite of with-only.
practice.why: A tool_used grader on Skill is normally only an indicator in a two-arm run. arm: both makes "it stayed quiet" part of the score in both arms.

practice.q: Which grader would you choose to check that a plan names the edge case "1,000 projects shows 25 rows on the first page"?

options.text: A regex grader for 1,?000 and 25 in the reply
options.why: The fact is exact and short, so a free regex checks it the same way every run, at no cost.

options.text: An llm grader: "PASS if the plan is good"
options.why: "Good" is not a checkable condition. A judge needs concrete PASS and FAIL conditions, and here a regex is cheaper and steadier.
That checks which tools Claude called, not what the plan says.

practice.q: Put one eval run of a case in order.
items: A fresh, isolated session starts with only the plugin under test loaded
It receives the case's prompt and works until it finishes or hits the turn limit
Each grader checks the reply, the tool calls or a file and passes or fails
The run's score is the weighted share of graders that passed
The case's score is the mean over its runs, with the plugin and without it
Δ is the with-plugin score minus the without-plugin score
practice.why: Runs are isolated so they cannot see each other; scores are averaged because one run of a model proves little; and only the difference with no plugin says what the plugin added.

practice.q: A grader must match "Frontend", "frontend" and "FRONTEND". Graders use JavaScript regular expressions. Fill in the field that makes the match ignore case.
practice.hint: The inline (?i) from Python does not work here.
practice.why: JavaScript has no inline (?i). The case-insensitive switch goes in flags: i, next to the pattern.
